extracted.intended_audience: Citizens (voters) of New York and delegates/participants in state ratifying conventions considering the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Federalist essays arguing for adoption of a single national government by enumerating the military, diplomatic, economic, and political dangers of disunion and the benefits of union. The texts present criteria for evaluating forms of government with historical examples and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: One government superior for defense
rubrics_metrics.description: One government can collect and avail itself of the talents and experience of the ablest men in whatever part of the Union they may be found; it can move on uniform principles of policy; it can harmonize, assimilate, and protect the several parts and members, and extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences cited: centralized ability to raise armies and fleets, coordinate defense rapidly, and avoid the inefficiencies and lack of concert that would attend multiple independent governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized treaty-making must consider whole and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the formation of treaties, [a national government] will regard the interest of the whole, and the particular interests of the parts as connected with that of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides conduct in foreign affairs so treaties are made with national consistency rather than conflicting state-by-state arrangements that could undermine common interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government can apply aggregate resources to defend any part
rubrics_metrics.description: It can apply the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any particular part, and that more easily and expeditiously than State governments or separate confederacies can possibly do, for want of concert and unity of system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts prompt, unified mobilization under one government with slow, disjointed aid among separate sovereignties; implies speed and unity are criteria for effective defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform militia organization under national authority increases efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: It can place the militia under one plan of discipline, and, by putting their officers in a proper line of subordination to the Chief Magistrate, will, as it were, consolidate them into one corps, and thereby render them more efficient than if divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific mechanism: unified discipline and chain of command consolidates disparate militias into an effective national force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into separate governments weakens sea and naval power
rubrics_metrics.description: Let England have its navigation and fleet... let those four of the constituent parts of the British empire be under four independent governments, and it is easy to perceive how soon they would each dwindle into comparative insignificance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the British example to argue that separate maritime policies and dispersed resources would prevent any part from sustaining a powerful fleet; warns division will reduce overall naval capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion invites foreign manipulation and diminishes international standing
rubrics_metrics.description: But whatever may be our situation... foreign nations will know and view it exactly as it is; and they will act toward us accordingly... If they find us either destitute of an effectual government... or split into... discordant republics... what a poor, pitiful figure will America make in their eyes!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: states could be courted, played off, or provoked by foreign powers; unity is a deterrent whereas division invites intrigue and outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union secures religion, liberty, property, and promotes prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: "An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities amongst yourselves... It must increase your strength, riches, and trade; and by this union... will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted counsel (Queen Anne) presented as an authoritative summation: political union produces internal peace and external strength; used as a standard for judging the benefits of union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division breeds jealousy, envy, and mutual distrust among neighboring confederacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Those gentlemen are greatly mistaken who suppose that alliances offensive and defensive might be formed between these confederacies... If any one of these nations or confederacies should rise... that moment would those neighbors behold her with envy and with fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that equality among neighboring sovereigns is unstable; unequal growth fuels jealousy and policies aimed at diminishing a neighbor's power—predicts recurring inter-state hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different commercial interests produce divergent treaties and conflicting alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of them would have its commerce with foreigners to regulate by distinct treaties; and as their productions and commodities are different... so would those treaties be essentially different... Different commercial concerns must create different interests, and of course different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: separate commercial policies will align states with different foreign powers, undermining collective defense and cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighboring nations are naturally enemies without confederation
rubrics_metrics.description: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames proximity as a structural source of conflict; used as an axiom to evaluate the risk of disunion among contiguous states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human passions and ambitions cause wars regardless of government form
rubrics_metrics.description: A man must be far gone in Utopian speculations who can seriously doubt that... the subdivisions into which they might be thrown would have frequent and violent contests... To presume a want of motives for such contests... would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Pericles, Wolsey, cardinal ambitions) support the general rule that personal ambition and passions drive states to conflict; assessment of government must account for human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial republics are not immune to war; commerce can both change and create motives for conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Has commerce hitherto done anything more than change the objects of war?... Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies?... Venice, Holland, Britain—commercial nations—have been frequently engaged in war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refutes the idea that commerce alone guarantees peace; uses historical record to evaluate claims that commercial interdependence prevents conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private passions of leaders and influential individuals can precipitate national wars
rubrics_metrics.description: There are others, not less numerous... which take their origin entirely in private passions; in the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals... Those who have but a superficial acquaintance... will themselves recollect a variety of instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Pericles and others; criterion: evaluate government vulnerability to manipulation by leaders' private motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial disputes (western lands) will be a fertile source of interstate hostility without a common umpire
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a vast tract of unsettled territory... a dismemberment of the Union... would revive this dispute... In the wide field of Western territory, therefore, we perceive an ample theatre for hostile pretensions, without any umpire or common judge to interpose between the contending parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Connecticut/Pennsylvania and Vermont disputes as precedent; emphasizes need for federal arbitration to avoid resort to force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition in commerce and protective/regulatory measures will provoke reprisals
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State... would pursue a system of commercial policy peculiar to itself. This would occasion distinctions, preferences, and exclusions... The infractions of these regulations, on one side, the efforts to prevent and repel them, on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, and these to reprisals and wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: New York imposing duties that burden Connecticut and New Jersey consumers; such impositions are assessed as likely to produce resistance and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan or geographic advantages create opportunities for domination and resentment
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey would afford an example... Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to be taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geographic/economic position as a criterion for potential inter-state friction and the need for neutral federal rules to prevent exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debt apportionment is a source of interstate collision
rubrics_metrics.description: The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. The apportionment... would be alike productive of ill-humor and animosity. How would it be possible to agree upon a rule of apportionment satisfactory to all?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that differing interests and creditor/debtor distributions make equitable apportionment contentious; non-compliance could produce bitter disputes and threaten peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a common judge/umpire encourages force as arbiter of disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: To reason from the past to the future, we shall have good ground to apprehend, that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: presence of impartial adjudicatory authority (federal courts) reduces risk of war; without it, states may resort to force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign alliances can become pretexts for conquest or undue influence
rubrics_metrics.description: How many conquests did the Romans and others make in the characters of allies, and what innovations did they under the same character introduce into the governments of those whom they pretended to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that inviting foreign troops/fleets as allies can lead to prolonged presence and domination; evaluates alliances for their long-term political risks, not only immediate benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: States may be seduced into neutrality or non-support by specious promises
rubrics_metrics.description: If one was attacked, would the others fly to its succor... Would there be no danger of their being flattered into neutrality by its specious promises, or seduced by a too great fondness for peace...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses reliability of interstate mutual defense absent central authority; highlights danger that states might decline to assist due to persuasion or self-interest.
